title: Constitution of India — Article 14 (Equality before law)
authority: Constituent Assembly of India / Government of India
summary: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. It is the foundation for challenging arbitrary or discriminatory action by state authorities.
text:
Article 14 of the Constitution of India provides that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

Practical significance: arbitrary action by a public authority — for example, unreasoned refusal of a licence, discriminatory treatment by a government office, or arbitrary inaction on a legitimate complaint — can be challenged as violative of Article 14 before the High Court under Article 226 (or the Supreme Court under Article 32 where a fundamental right is directly involved).

Article 14 applies to 'State' action; purely private disputes are generally addressed through ordinary civil, criminal or consumer remedies rather than constitutional writs.

title: Constitution of India — Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty)
authority: Constituent Assembly of India / Government of India
summary: Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Supreme Court jurisprudence has read into it rights to livelihood, dignity, shelter and a speedy fair process.
text:
Article 21 of the Constitution of India states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

Through judicial interpretation, Article 21 embraces the right to live with human dignity, the right to livelihood, protection against cruel and degrading treatment, and fair procedure before deprivation of liberty. It is central to habeas corpus petitions (against unlawful detention), challenges to custodial violence, and petitions protecting victims of violence or harassment where state protection is sought.

Where personal liberty is at immediate risk, the appropriate urgent remedies are approaching the nearest police, the High Court (writ jurisdiction), or the National/State Legal Services Authority for free urgent legal aid.

title: Constitution of India — Article 32 (Right to constitutional remedies — Supreme Court)
authority: Constituent Assembly of India / Government of India
summary: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court power to issue writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto) for enforcement of fundamental rights, and is itself a fundamental right.
text:
Article 32 of the Constitution of India confers on the Supreme Court the power to issue directions, orders or writs — including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto — which may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III (fundamental rights). The right to move the Supreme Court is itself guaranteed as a fundamental right.

Practical note: for most citizens' grievances, the High Court under Article 226 is the more accessible constitutional forum because it is geographically nearer and its writ power extends beyond fundamental rights. Article 32 petitions are generally reserved for direct violations of fundamental rights.

title: Constitution of India — Article 226 (Writ powers of High Courts)
authority: Constituent Assembly of India / Government of India
summary: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose — a broader jurisdiction than Article 32, commonly used against inaction or arbitrariness of public authorities, including police refusal to act.
text:
Article 226 of the Constitution of India empowers every High Court to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases any Government, directions, orders or writs — including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto — for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

Because the power extends to 'any other purpose', a writ petition under Article 226 is a standard remedy against: refusal or inaction of a public authority (mandamus), unlawful detention (habeas corpus), quashing of illegal orders (certiorari), and arbitrary administrative action read with Article 14.

A citizen aggrieved by, for example, a police station's refusal to register a cognizable offence may, after escalating to the Superintendent of Police and approaching the Magistrate, move the High Court under Article 226 seeking a direction to register and investigate.

title: Constitution of India — Article 39A (Equal justice and free legal aid)
authority: Constituent Assembly of India / Government of India
summary: Article 39A directs the State to provide free legal aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities — the constitutional basis of NALSA and District Legal Services Authorities.
text:
Article 39A of the Constitution of India provides that the State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

This directive principle is implemented through the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987: the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs) and District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) provide free legal advice, panel lawyers and, in eligible cases, free representation. The NALSA helpline is 15100.

Any litigant who cannot afford a lawyer should approach the DLSA at the district court complex.

title: Constitution of India — Article 300A (No deprivation of property save by authority of law)
authority: Constituent Assembly of India / Government of India
summary: Article 300A provides that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law — the constitutional anchor for property and possession disputes against unlawful dispossession.
text:
Article 300A of the Constitution of India states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. After the Forty-fourth Amendment, the right to property ceased to be a fundamental right but remains a constitutional right.

Practical significance: a person dispossessed of property otherwise than in accordance with law — whether by a private party or a state authority — may seek recovery of possession through civil courts, and in appropriate cases specific relief under the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Dispossession without legal authority is actionable.
